blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Defining and using procedures; where a procedure is appropriate; parameters, by value and by reference; and defining and using functions.

blocks.heading: Procedures: definition, call, placement
blocks.text:
A procedure is a module that does one named job and hands back no value through its name. Its definition:

```pseudocode
PROCEDURE GreetCustomer(Name : STRING)
   OUTPUT "Welcome, ", Name
ENDPROCEDURE
```

The header names the module and its parameters; ENDPROCEDURE closes it. Its call is a statement on its own: CALL GreetCustomer("Anna") - the call does the job, and nothing is left over to assign, because a procedure returns nothing through its name. Where a procedure belongs in the construction of an algorithm is the design question, and it has two answers. Where the same job is needed in several places: printing a receipt header, greeting a caller, drawing a menu border - written once as a procedure and called by name, the job is maintained in one place, so a change to the greeting is a change to one module. Where the program is a long sequence of named steps: a payroll run decomposes into ReadTimes, CalculatePay, PrintPayslips - each step a procedure, the main program reads as the plan, and each module is small enough to check on its own. A procedure is also where the module's job ends with an action rather than an answer - printing, saving, showing - which is the first hint of the procedure-function split that follows. A design habit keeps the placement honest: when a program is planned on paper, each named step of the plan is a candidate module, and the test for candidacy is repetition or length - a step that appears twice in the plan, or a step whose body runs to a page, is written as a procedure and its line in the plan becomes a call. The plan then reads at two levels: the main program as a list of calls, the modules as the detail beneath each - which is exactly the two-level shape 12.2's structure charts draw, arrived at from the writing side.

blocks.heading: Parameters and arguments
blocks.text: A module's values arrive through its parameters - and through nothing else. A parameter is a variable named in the header: PROCEDURE ReportStall(StallName : STRING, TakingsToday : REAL) - and the argument is the value the caller passes in the call: CALL ReportStall("Spices", 435.50). The rule with teeth: the values a module works on arrive through its parameters, so INPUT inside a module is the wrong place for the module's data - the header already holds every value as a parameter, and the call already supplies them. A parameter is passed by value or by reference, and the difference is who owns the variable. By value, the module receives a copy: it may change the parameter inside, and the caller's variable keeps its own value, because the caller handed over a copy. By reference, the module works on the caller's variable itself: a change inside shows outside the call, which is how a procedure that computes an answer can hand it back - write the result into a reference parameter and the caller's variable now holds it. In pseudocode the keyword stands in front of the parameter it governs: PROCEDURE Deposit(BYVAL Amount : REAL, BYREF ClubTotal : REAL) passes Amount by value and ClubTotal by reference, and a parameter written with neither keyword is passed by value. The choice is design: values that only feed the module pass by value, protected from stray changes; values the module must fill in for the caller pass by reference, because the caller is waiting to receive the result. The parameter list is also a contract the caller can check: the number of arguments must match the number of parameters, the types must match in order, and the caller's variable for a reference parameter must exist before the call. A call that passes two arguments to a three-parameter module, or a string where an integer stands in the header, is caught by reading the header alone - which is why the header is called the interface in the next unit's terms: it is where the two sides meet and where every mismatch is visible.

blocks.heading: Functions
blocks.text:
A function is a module that computes a single value and hands it back through its name. Its definition:

```pseudocode
FUNCTION AreaOfRoof(Length : REAL, Width : REAL) RETURNS REAL
   DECLARE Area : REAL
   Area <- Length * Width
   RETURN Area
ENDFUNCTION
```

The header names the module, its parameters and the type of the returned value; RETURN inside the body sends the value back and ends the function; ENDFUNCTION closes it. The use is the difference from a procedure: a function is used in an expression - the call is replaced by the returned value - so it is assigned, RoofArea <- AreaOfRoof(6.5, 4.2), tested, IF AreaOfRoof(L, W) > 20 THEN, or joined into a larger expression, and it never follows CALL, because CALL names a job and a function's call is a value. OUTPUT inside a function is the same fault wearing a different coat: the caller needs the value, so the body RETURNs it - displaying it does the caller no good, because OUTPUT goes to the screen and the caller's expression gets nothing. A function is appropriate exactly where a value must be computed and used: the fee for a weight, the average of an array, the larger of two readings - any question the program asks whose answer belongs in an expression. A function also earns its place in a test: because the call is a value, the condition can be written straight against it - IF ParcelFee(Weight) > 50 THEN reads as one question - and a function used in a test is a function that can be reused in a print, a save and a further computation without ever being rewritten. That is the compound interest of returning values: each caller that needs the fee gets it from one module, so the rule itself is stated once and lives once, and every change to the fee - a new threshold, a new rate - is one change in one body.

blocks.heading: Common errors
blocks.text: Three slips recur. OUTPUT where a function must RETURN: the caller needs the value, so the body RETURNs it - the test is whether the calling code needs the value, because a displayed value is nothing to assign. INPUT inside a module: the values arrive through the parameters - the test is the header, because every parameter is already a value. And CALLing a function or assigning a procedure's result: a procedure is CALLed as a statement, a function is used in an expression - the test is whether the module returns a value, because a value-returning module never follows CALL.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The modules here are what 9.1's decomposition produced and what 9.2's constructs fill; the identifier rules and the insert's functions are 11.1's subject; the loops these modules carry walk 10.2's arrays and read 10.3's files, and 12.2 designs with these modules named.
